This is the section you keep open on 17 October. Everything else on this page is preparation. This is execution — clock, triage, opening moves per domain, and the copy-paste kit.

The twelve hours

WindowPhaseWhat happens
09:00 – 09:30TriageRead every challenge once. Tag each with a domain. Sort by the attack order in Section 2. Do not solve anything yet.
09:30 – 13:30Priority 1 — Misc, Stego, OSINTThe three fastest-scoring domains. Work them in that order, moving between them freely.
13:30 – 16:30Priority 2 — Web, Crypto, AI/LLMBasic Web, then basic Crypto, then AI/LLM. Keep to basics; skip anything that smells like a research problem.
16:30 – 18:30Priority 3 — Cloud, ForensicsCloud first: it is usually two commands. Then Forensics, which is slower but mechanical.
18:30 – 20:30Priority 4 — Reverse, PwnBasic reversing only. For Pwn, attempt ret2win and nothing else. Hard cap both.
20:30 – 21:00Final sweepRe-read every unsolved Easy. Verify every flag you have banked. Submit nothing unverified.

Step 1 — triage (09:00–09:30, do not solve anything)

Read the whole board before you touch a keyboard. The most expensive mistake available is solving the first easy-looking challenge you see. You cannot allocate twelve hours sensibly against a contest you have not read.
  1. Open every challenge — Expand all ten categories. Read every title and description once, without trying to solve any of them.
  2. Tag each one — Write a domain letter next to each: M, S, O, W, C, A, CL, F, R, P. If you genuinely cannot tell, tag it M — Misc is the default.
  3. Mark the obvious ones — Put a star next to anything whose solution you can already see. Those are your first hour after triage.
  4. Note the point values — If points are shown, sort within each domain by value ascending. Cheap flags first, always.
  5. Count what you have — Ten domains, N challenges. Write the counts. You are now allocating twelve hours against a known inventory instead of guessing.
  6. Then, and only then, start — Begin with the starred Misc challenges.

Step 2 — the universal flag method

Run the cheapest check first, every time, before you think. This is the single biggest difference between teams that score and teams that do not.
  1. Read the description twice — CTF descriptions are written deliberately. Words like hidden, buried, deleted, forgotten, somewhere in, without opening — each is pointing at a technique. Underline them.
  2. Click every hint — In practice there is no penalty. Hints exist to teach. On the 17th they may cost points, so learn the patterns now.
  3. Get the file onto Linux — Right-click the download link, copy the link address, then wget it into the shell. Left-clicking downloads it to your own machine instead.
  4. Run file first. Always. — People waste hours running stego tools on a text file and grep on a PNG. One second prevents it.
  5. Try the cheap five — strings, then grep -o 'picoCTF{.*}', then exiftool, then binwalk, then file again. Each takes seconds. This resolves most easy challenges.
  6. Decode, never guess — Base64, hex, ROT13, reversed, URL-encoded: use CyberChef. Do not attempt it mentally.
  7. Automate the last resort — Images: Aperi'Solve or zsteg -a. Archives: binwalk -e. Disks: fls and icat.
  8. Write it down — Challenge name plus the command that worked, in one notes file. That file is your most valuable possession by hour ten.
  9. Thirty minutes, then switch — No progress in thirty minutes: stop, switch, return later. This is in the official guide for a reason.

Step 3 — the copy-paste kit

open these first — every domain, in order of cost
# 1. the cheap five, on EVERY artifact (30 seconds)
$ file x; strings x | grep -i pico; exiftool x; binwalk x

# 2. recursive flag grep across everything downloaded
$ grep -rio 'picoCTF{.*}' .

# 3. web: the 30-second checklist
$ curl -s $URL/robots.txt; curl -I $URL
$ curl -s $URL | grep -i pico

# 4. crypto: classify before you think (2 minutes)
$ python3 -c "print(int(open('n.txt').read()).bit_length())"
#   then paste n into factordb.com

# 5. cloud: two commands, no credentials needed
$ aws s3 ls s3://<bucket> --no-sign-request
$ curl http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/

# 6. reversing: strings before Ghidra, always
$ strings ./bin | grep -i pico; checksec ./bin; upx -d ./bin

# 7. pwn: read, check, ret2win — then stop
$ checksec ./bin && python3 pwn_template.py offset ./bin

Step 4 — opening moves, domain by domain

Work in this order. Move between domains freely, but never finish one domain before starting the next.
01MiscellaneousPriority 1
Sort Misc by point value ascending and do the cheapest three first. For any file: file → strings → grep -rio 'picoCTF{.*}' . For any nc challenge: connect and read before you think.
cap 20 minutes per challenge90 min
02SteganographyPriority 1
file — confirm what it really is before anything else. exiftool &lt;img&gt;, then strings &lt;img&gt; | grep -i pico. If it is SVG, HTML or PDF: read the source with cat and grep for text elements.
cap 15 minutes75 min
03OSINTPriority 1
Run exiftool on any image first — GPS is occasionally free. Go straight to three reverse-image engines. Do not ration yourself to Google. For a handle: sherlock, then read the profiles it finds.
cap 15 minutes per question45 min
04Web ExploitationPriority 2
Ctrl+U on the page, then curl it and grep — never rely on the rendered view alone. Check robots.txt, /.git/config, /admin and editor backups. Inspect cookies; try flipping any boolean-looking value.
cap 25 minutes per challenge75 min
05CryptographyPriority 2
Identify whether it is an encoding or a cipher. Encodings have no key — just decode them. For RSA: check e first, then try factordb on n. Two minutes, then decide. For anything classical: paste into CyberChef and let Magic try everything.
cap 20 minutes60 min
06AI / LLM SecurityPriority 2
Ask for the system prompt first, before anything else. It takes thirty seconds. If refused, ask for a translation, a summary, or a completion instead. For the flag itself, ask for an encoding rather than the literal string.
cap 15 minutes45 min
07Cloud SecurityPriority 3
Look for a bucket name in the source, then try --no-sign-request immediately. Look for any URL-fetching feature. If you find one, go straight to 169.254.169.254. Check /latest/user-data/ — developers leave secrets there constantly.
cap 20 minutes45 min
08Digital ForensicsPriority 3
file, then immediately strings &lt;artifact&gt; | grep -i pico. For a pcap: open in Wireshark, Follow TCP Stream, cycle through. For a disk: mmls → fls → icat, and grep everything once mounted.
cap 30 minutes75 min
09Reverse EngineeringPriority 4
file, then strings &lt;binary&gt; | grep -i pico. Always. If it is Python or Java, decompile — you will be reading near-source. If it is C, run ltrace and strace before you reach for gdb.
cap 25 minutes60 min
10PwnPriority 4
strings first. Then read the source — Pwn challenges hand it to you. Look for an uncalled win() function. If one exists, this is ret2win and it is worth doing. Use pwn_template.py offset to find the padding, then ret2win to build the payload.
cap 45 minutes for the entire domain45 min

Step 5 — when you are stuck

If you have been stuck for…Do this
Under 5 minutesKeep going. This is normal. Re-read the description — the wording almost always names the technique.
5–15 minutesRun the cheap five again on the artifact. Most 'hard' challenges are a cheap check nobody ran.
15–30 minutesClick the hint if one exists. Then try the escalation ladder for that domain, in order.
30–45 minutesSearch the exact error message or tool name. Someone has hit it.
Over 45 minutesSwitch challenge. You are past the cap. Note what you tried in your scratch file and move to the next domain in the order.
Over 60 minutesAbandon and do not return. Write one line: what it looked like, what failed. Revisit only in the 20:30 sweep.

Step 6 — the seven discipline rules

  1. Triage before you solve — The first thirty minutes are read-only. You cannot allocate time sensibly across a day you have not looked at.
  2. Thirty minutes, then switch — No progress in thirty minutes: move to another challenge. This is in the official guide. Treat it as a rule, not a suggestion.
  3. Never finish a domain before starting the next — Work the sequence, but abandon a domain the moment it stops yielding. Half of everything beats all of one thing.
  4. Submit the instant you have a flag — Points count when submitted, not when found. Do not batch them. Do not hold one back to double-check later.
  5. Keep something in the oven — When you stall on a hard challenge, start an easy one in parallel rather than staring. Momentum matters more than stubbornness.
  6. Write down every command that worked — One notes file, open all day. By hour ten you will be re-running things you solved at hour two and cannot recall.
  7. Eat, drink, stand up — A twelve-hour round is an endurance event. A rested beginner consistently beats a fried expert.

Step 7 — the final thirty minutes (20:30–21:00)

Stop opening new challenges. In the last block:
  1. Re-attempt anything you were close on — fresh eyes beat persistence.
  2. Run the cheap five against every file you have not run them on.
  3. Try the flag-format grep across your whole download folder.
  4. Verify every flag is actually submitted. An unsubmitted flag scores zero.

Submitting a flag

A flag is a unique string proving you solved the challenge, usually picoCTF{...}. Paste it into the scoring service exactly as found — including the wrapper and the case. There is no penalty for a wrong guess, so submit the moment something looks right. Check the challenge statement for a custom wrapper before assuming the format.

01Miscellaneous0/6
Encoding chains
Layered base64, hex, ROT13 and custom encodings that must be peeled in order.
Shell trickery
Files with awkward names, hidden files, permission puzzles and find-by-property.
Script reading
A supplied Python or shell script whose output you must predict or repair.
Esoteric &amp; logic
Puzzles that reward structured thinking over tooling.
Network warm-ups
Connect with nc and read what the server tells you.
Cross-discipline
Two categories fused — a stego file that needs a crypto key, and similar.
02Steganography0/6
Concatenated files
A second file appended after the end of the first, or embedded after the image EOF marker. Recoverable with binwalk or a simple carve.
LSB encoding
Data written into the least significant bits of pixel values, recoverable with zsteg, stegsolve or a few lines of Python and Pillow.
Spectrogram and audio
Text or shapes encoded in the frequency domain of an audio file, visible in a spectrogram but completely inaudible on playback.
Tool-specific carriers
Data hidden using steghide in JPEGs or WAV, outguess in JPEGs, or OpenStego — each requiring its matching extraction tool.
Container manipulation
Hidden data in PNG ancillary chunks, JPEG comments, PDF metadata or font tables — legitimate container features used off-purpose.
Encoding layers
A flag that is itself base64 or hex encoded, sitting inside something already extracted. Layers are common and cheap to check.
03OSINT0/6
Metadata extraction
EXIF data from images, document properties, PDF metadata and camera serial numbers that identify a device, a location or a photographer.
Geolocation
Fixing a position from visual evidence: signage, road markings, terrain, sun position, weather, licence plates and architectural style.
Username & account hunting
Tracing one handle across platforms using archived pages, cached profiles and search operators, then confirming an identity from what they have in common.
Archived web content
Recovering pages from the Wayback Machine to expose information the live site has since removed, or to date when something was published.
Public record research
Company registries, professional listings, public tender records and academic papers used to confirm or refute a claimed affiliation.
Data aggregation
Several weak public sources combining into one strong conclusion — a common correlation a visual check alone would not have caught.
04Web Exploitation0/6
Injection flaws
SQL injection across stacked and blind variants, NoSQL injection, command injection and LDAP injection — where unescaped input reaches an interpreter and executes as code.
Cross-site scripting
Reflected, stored and DOM-based XSS, with realistic sinks: search fields, profile inputs, URL fragments and JSON responses reflected straight into client-side JavaScript.
Access control
IDOR through predictable identifiers, broken object-level authorisation, insecure direct object references and privilege escalation from a low-privilege account.
Server-side request forgery
Servers that fetch attacker-supplied URLs — including a cloud metadata endpoint in the final stages — turning an outbound request into a credential theft primitive.
Authentication & session
Weak session handling, predictable password resets, forgeable tokens and login flows that can be bypassed by editing a single request header.
Logic & race conditions
Discount stacking, negative-quantity purchases, race conditions between competing requests and business rules that were never written to be enforced.
05Cryptography0/6
Classical ciphers
Vigenère, substitution and transposition ciphers broken by frequency analysis, Kasiski examination or crib dragging rather than by brute force.
RSA and public-key
Shared primes, small exponents, textbook padding, faulty signature checks and key-recovery attacks where the modulus leaks through timing or randomness.
Symmetric ciphers
AES in ECB mode, reused nonces, short keys and known-plaintext attacks against block ciphers used outside the way they were designed for.
Hashing & password security
Weak hash functions, unsalted digests, length-extension attacks and password hashes that can be attacked faster than brute force.
PGP & key handling
Key generation with poor entropy, messages encrypted to the wrong key, detached signatures that can be stripped or replayed.
Encoding traps
Base64, hex and custom encodings that look like security but provide none, layered over a real cipher that does the actual work.
06AI / LLM Security0/6
Direct prompt injection
Overriding system instructions through crafted user input, instruction-collision attacks and role-play framing designed to bypass refusal behaviour.
Indirect prompt injection
Instructions hidden in content the model retrieves — a webpage, a document, an image, an email — so the model treats attacker text as trusted context.
Tool & agent abuse
Coaxing an LLM with tool access into calling the wrong function, passing unvalidated arguments, or exfiltrating context it should never have surfaced.
Data & model poisoning
Manipulating training or retrieval data so a model produces a targeted wrong answer, recovers a memorised secret, or behaves differently under a trigger phrase.
Sensitive data exposure
Prompting a model until it reveals system prompts, embedded secrets, cross-tenant context or information it was configured never to disclose.
Guardrail evasion
Encoding tricks, token-level manipulation, adversarial suffixes and multi-turn escalation that defeat output filters while preserving the objective.
07Cloud Security0/6
Storage misconfiguration
Buckets and containers exposed to anonymous list or read, overly permissive object ACLs, and backup archives left readable.
IAM & privilege abuse
Over-broad role policies, trust relationships that accept unexpected principals, and privilege escalation chains through role assumption.
Metadata services
Instance and function metadata endpoints abused to steal temporary credentials — the same technique behind real-world cloud compromises.
Exposed secrets
API keys, access keys and connection strings leaked in environment variables, logs, source control or error messages.
Containers & orchestration
Dockerfiles and manifests with excessive capabilities, host mounts, privileged mode or missing security context.
Network exposure
Open security groups, public load balancers and management interfaces reachable from the public internet.
08Digital Forensics0/6
Disk & filesystem
Partition tables, deleted file recovery, unallocated space, alternate data streams, journal artefacts and files that were renamed rather than deleted.
Memory forensics
Process and network state recovered from a RAM dump: running processes, injected code, open handles, credentials and injected shellcode in memory.
Network analysis
PCAP files reassembled into sessions — reconstructing a web request, spotting data exfiltration over DNS, or identifying a command-and-control channel.
Timeline reconstruction
Correlating timestamps across artefacts to answer "when did this happen", where file times, log entries and registry keys disagree with one another.
Embedded & hidden data
Data appended after the end of a file, buried in slack space, hidden in image metadata or packed inside another container that the header does not describe.
Log & registry analysis
Windows event logs, browser history and caches, and registry keys that record user actions no other artefact captured.
09Reverse Engineering0/6
Flag checks
The classic form: a routine compares your input against a transformed value. You recover the transformation, invert it, and recover the flag.
Obfuscated control flow
Opaque predicates, flattened dispatch tables and switch tables inserted specifically to defeat decompilers, requiring manual reconstruction of the real logic.
Packed and encrypted payloads
Binaries whose meaningful code is unpacked at runtime, so static analysis shows a stub. You need to dump the process after the unpacking stage completes.
Anti-analysis
Timing checks, debugger detection and environment probes that must be identified and bypassed before the real logic will run.
Embedded data
Flags or keys embedded as byte arrays, decoded by a small routine buried somewhere in a large binary. The reverse part is locating the decoder.
Algorithm reimplementation
Custom hash, compression or cipher routines you must reimplement in another language to compute a comparison value or decrypt a blob.
10Pwn0/6
Stack overflows
Classic buffer overflows where a long input overwrites the saved return address. The foundation skill, and still the basis of most easy challenges.
ROP chains
Return-oriented programming to defeat non-executable stacks — chaining gadgets to call execve("/bin/sh", NULL, NULL) without ever executing injected shellcode.
Format string bugs
Unvalidated format specifiers in printf leaking stack memory or granting an arbitrary write through %n. Enormous information leak for comparatively little effort.
Heap exploitation
Use-after-free, double free and off-by-one bugs against ptmalloc, requiring careful reasoning about chunk metadata and allocator state.
Mitigation bypass
Defeating ASLR, stack canaries, NX and RELRO — by leaking a libc address, or by finding a function that discloses the canary for us.
Race conditions
TOCTOU bugs where a check and a use are separated in time, exploited with threads or by winning the scheduling window.

Formatting rules that apply everywhere

  1. Copy the entire string — picoCTF{, the contents, and the closing }. Not just the part inside the braces.
  2. No leading or trailing spaces. Select carefully; a trailing space is the single most common rejection. If in doubt, paste into a text editor first and trim.
  3. Case-sensitive. Do not capitalise or lowercase anything.
  4. No quotes. If you wrapped it in quotes for a shell command, strip them.
  5. Underscores and dashes are part of it. Do not tidy them up.

If it is rejected and you are sure it is right

  1. Re-read the challenge statement — some challenges use a custom wrapper instead of picoCTF{}.
  2. Re-run the extraction. A partial flag usually means you stopped one step early in an encoding chain.
  3. Check for a second flag in the same file. Some challenges hide more than one, and only one is accepted.
  4. On CyLab, try refreshing the challenge page — stale sessions occasionally reject a perfectly good flag.

What to do immediately after it scores

  1. Record it. One line in your notes file: challenge name, the command that produced it, the flag. You will not remember at hour ten.
  2. Note the technique, not just the answer. What did you run that worked? That pattern is what transfers to the next challenge.
  3. Submit it immediately. An unsubmitted flag scores zero — this is the most common way teams lose points they already earned.
  4. Then move on. Do not celebrate for twenty minutes. The next cheap flag is usually thirty seconds away.

Using AI — the honest answer

Can you use AI on Ghost Protocol CTF 2.0?

Not addressed by the organisers. No published rule permits or forbids it - so the safe default is: do not use it to solve challenges.

  1. What the organisers have published — Nothing. There is no rules page on gpctf2.0.cyberinvaders.tech - /rules, /guidelines, /about, /terms and /conduct all return 404. The full code of conduct appears only on the Unstop listing, and it does not mention AI, LLMs, ChatGPT or any equivalent.
  2. What the code of conduct DOES forbid — Sharing flags, write-ups, solutions or hints with other teams. Attacking anything outside the provided environment. DoS and brute-forcing the infrastructure. Exploiting the scoring system. None of these mentions AI - but an AI solving a challenge for you sits in the same philosophical territory as receiving a solution from someone else.
  3. The complication: AI/LLM Security is a category — One of the ten domains is AI/LLM Security, covering prompt injection and model abuse. For that category to function, interaction with models is clearly contemplated. But that is about ATTACKING models, not about using one to answer a Crypto challenge.
  4. What other CTFs decided in 2026 — The community is split. skateboarding dog CTF 2026 and LakeCTF ban AI outright. PwnSec CTF 2026 runs two leaderboards - Human and Cyborg - where Human teams may use AI only as a search engine. DEF CON CTF Qualifiers 2026 permitted AI but forbade using it to solve a challenge outright. DiceCTF 2026 and Grey CTF published no policy at all, which functioned as permissive by default.
  5. The practical recommendation — Treat AI as a search engine, not as a teammate. Looking up 'zsteg bit-plane syntax' is materially the same as searching a man page or Stack Overflow, and is almost certainly fine. Pasting a challenge description, a ciphertext or a binary and asking for the solution is not - it is asking something else to solve the challenge for you. If you would not paste it to another competitor, do not paste it to a model.
  6. How to be certain — Ask in the official announcement channel before 09:00 on 17 October. That channel is where the organisers publish rule updates, and a five-second question removes a disqualification risk that is far larger than any flag.
Verdict — Use it to look up syntax you already understand. Do not use it to solve, explain or reverse a challenge. When in doubt, ask the organisers first.
SituationVerdictReasoning
Looking up tool syntax or a flag formatAlmost certainly fineEquivalent to reading documentation. You still do the work.
Asking for an explanation of a concept (what is ECB mode)Fine - and do it now, not on the 17thThis is learning. Do it during 14-16 Oct so it costs you nothing on the day.
Debugging your own script's Python errorFineIt is your script and your logic. Standard development practice.
Pasting a challenge description and asking how to solve itDo notThis is asking for the solution. Sits next to the flag-sharing prohibition.
Pasting a ciphertext, hash or extracted data and asking for the answerDo notIdentical to the above, just with more steps.
Uploading a challenge binary and asking what it doesDo notThis is outsourcing the reversing, which is the entire skill being tested.
Letting an agentic tool connect to a challenge serverDo notAgentic tools acting on the competition infrastructure is the clearest violation pattern in 2026 CTF policy.
Generating a full solver script from the challenge textDo notThe output is the solution, regardless of who typed it.
Practising with AI during 14-16 OctYes - strongly encouragedNothing restricts preparation. Learn freely now so you need it less on the day.

Organised byCyber Invaders · NIET Greater Noida

What kind of CTF this is

What it means
Jeopardy-style, not attack-and-defenceYou are given a board of challenges across ten categories. Each solved challenge yields a flag string that you submit to a scoring service. You are never defending anything — there is no live infrastructure of your own to protect.
Two phases, and only the first matters right nowPhase 01 is a 12-hour remote Jeopardy round on 17 October, open pan-India. Phase 02 is a 12-hour on-ground finale at NIET Greater Noida on 24 October. Qualifying for Phase 02 is the entire objective of the next three days.
Dynamic scoringFlags are scored dynamically, which in practice means a challenge's value falls as more teams solve it. Early flags on uncommon categories are worth proportionally more — this is the argument for attempting the domains other teams skip.
Difficulty skews hard, by the organisers' own admissionEvery official category page repeats that challenges are “weighted toward the mid and upper difficulty bands.” Plan for breadth, not for heroics.

What you can do

PermittedBasis
Use any software you likeThe organiser tool lists name Burp Suite, sqlmap, ffuf, Ghidra, pwntools, Volatility and similar by name. Tooling is expected, not restricted.
Search the internetEvery category page recommends public learning resources and prior research as preparation.
Work as a team of 1–3Solo entry is explicitly permitted, so you may compete alone if needed.
Use public writeups for learning nowThe preparation advice across all ten categories points at public material.

Not stated — use judgement

These are not covered by any published rule. Treat each as a risk to be weighed, not a permission. When in doubt, do not.
UnaddressedWhy it is uncertain
AI assistance during the roundNot addressed in any published material. For an AI/LLM category to be meaningful, some interaction with models is evidently contemplated — but whether you may use one to solve a Crypto challenge is simply not stated.
Sharing flags between teamsNo published rule found. Universally forbidden in Jeopardy CTFs and carries real disqualification risk.
Attacking the scoring infrastructureNo published rule found. Universally forbidden and, again, a disqualification risk.

The ClockThe ClockThe Clock

The twelve-hour allocation

WindowPhaseWhat happensWhy this position
09:00 – 09:30TriageRead every challenge once. Tag each with a domain. Sort by the attack order in Section 2. Do not solve anything yet.Solving the first easy thing you see is the most expensive mistake available. Thirty minutes of reading buys you the whole day.
09:30 – 13:30Priority 1 — Misc, Stego, OSINTThe three fastest-scoring domains. Work them in that order, moving between them freely.These need the least specialist knowledge and yield the most points per minute. Banking a floor early changes how calmly you play the rest of the day.
13:30 – 16:30Priority 2 — Web, Crypto, AI/LLMBasic Web, then basic Crypto, then AI/LLM. Keep to basics; skip anything that smells like a research problem.Each has a small set of high-frequency bugs. Learn those and you collect the easy points without touching the hard ones.
16:30 – 18:30Priority 3 — Cloud, ForensicsCloud first: it is usually two commands. Then Forensics, which is slower but mechanical.Cloud looks exotic and is not. Forensics is methodical — it rewards patience rather than insight.
18:30 – 20:30Priority 4 — Reverse, PwnBasic reversing only. For Pwn, attempt ret2win and nothing else. Hard cap both.These are the domains the official guide tells you to deprioritise. Respect that: an hour here usually buys less than an hour spent re-checking earlier work.
20:30 – 21:00Final sweepRe-read every unsolved Easy. Verify every flag you have banked. Submit nothing unverified.Fatigue makes you sloppy. A calm final pass routinely recovers two or three flags you walked past at hour three.

The seven rules

Rule
1Triage before you solve — The first thirty minutes are read-only. You cannot allocate time sensibly across a day you have not looked at.
2Thirty minutes, then switch — No progress in thirty minutes: move to another challenge. This is in the official guide. Treat it as a rule, not a suggestion.
3Never finish a domain before starting the next — Work the sequence, but abandon a domain the moment it stops yielding. Half of everything beats all of one thing.
4Submit the instant you have a flag — Points count when submitted, not when found. Do not batch them. Do not hold one back to double-check later.
5Keep something in the oven — When you stall on a hard challenge, start an easy one in parallel rather than staring. Momentum matters more than stubbornness.
6Write down every command that worked — One notes file, open all day. By hour ten you will be re-running things you solved at hour two and cannot recall.
7Eat, drink, stand up — A twelve-hour round is an endurance event. A rested beginner consistently beats a fried expert.

The opening thirty minutes

Triage, not solving. The most expensive mistake available is solving the first easy-looking challenge you see. You cannot allocate twelve hours sensibly against a contest you have not read.
  1. Open every challenge — Expand all ten categories. Read every title and description once, without trying to solve any of them.
  2. Tag each one — Write a domain letter next to each: M, S, O, W, C, A, CL, F, R, P. If you genuinely cannot tell, tag it M — Misc is the default.
  3. Mark the obvious ones — Put a star next to anything whose solution you can already see. Those are your first hour after triage.
  4. Note the point values — If points are shown, sort within each domain by value ascending. Cheap flags first, always.
  5. Count what you have — Ten domains, N challenges. Write the counts. You are now allocating twelve hours against a known inventory instead of guessing.
  6. Then, and only then, start — Begin with the starred Misc challenges.

Why breadth wins here

Every official category page repeats that challenges are “weighted toward the mid and upper difficulty bands.” That single sentence should shape the entire day: attempt broadly, bank everything cheap, and cap the expensive domains hard. Ten shallow attempts beat two deep ones when most challenges are hard by design.

Attack OrderAttack OrderAttack Order

The sequence

#DomainTierBudgetWhy here
01MiscPriority 190 minHighest volume, lowest specialist knowledge. The floor of your score is built here.
02StegoPriority 175 minNamed the fastest-scoring domain in the official guide. Do it while you are still fresh.
03OSINTPriority 145 minQuick if you know the three reverse-image engines; a trap if you do not.
04WebPriority 275 minView source, robots.txt, cookies. Reliable, well-rehearsed points.
05CryptoPriority 260 minEncodings and classical ciphers only. Leave RSA alone unless it looks trivial.
06AI / LLMPriority 245 minSystem prompt extraction is thirty seconds for a flag. Never skip it.
07CloudPriority 345 minTwo commands: public bucket, metadata endpoint. Exotic reputation, trivial execution.
08ForensicsPriority 375 minMethodical and slower. Mechanical once you know the workflow.
09ReversePriority 460 minBasic only. If it needs a debugger for more than twenty minutes, stop.
10PwnPriority 445 minHard cap. ret2win only. Abandon without guilt — the guide says so explicitly.

Why this order

01–03Fastest scoring first
Misc, Stego and OSINT need the least specialist knowledge and yield the most points per minute.
04–06Known bugs, rehearsed
Web, Crypto and AI/LLM each have a small set of high-frequency weaknesses. Learn those and you collect the easy points without touching the research-grade ones.
07–08Mechanical, slower
Cloud is usually two commands. Forensics is methodical — it rewards patience and a fixed routine rather than insight.
09–10Capped deliberately
Reverse basic only. Pwn gets ret2win and nothing else. The official guidance is explicit and it is correct.
Single points of failure. Cloud, OSINT, Forensics and Reverse each have exactly one place to practise. If any of those sites is down, you cannot train that domain at all — which is why they are scheduled on day three, with time left to react.

MethodologyMethodologyMethodology

How to read this. Each domain has five numbered steps. Steps 01–02 are almost always recognition. Steps 03–04 are technique. Step 05 is nearly always muscle memory. If you only have time for one thing per domain, do step 01.

01 Miscellaneous Priority 1 open domain

01
Learn to recognise encodings on sight: base64 ends in =, hex is 0-9 a-f, ROT13 keeps English word-shape.
02
Make file and strings automatic first moves on every artifact you touch.
03
Keep CyberChef open in a tab. The Magic operation resolves most encoding chains without thought.
04
Never brute-force a 25-key cipher by hand when a five-line loop will do it.
05
Get comfortable with the shell: find by name, size, owner and permission solves a surprising share of these.
Tools the organisers name for Miscellaneous
CyberChefPython 3stringsgrepfilexxdncbase64

02 Steganography Priority 1 open domain

01
Memorise the escalation ladder: file → strings → binwalk → exiftool → zsteg → steghide. Trying them in order beats guessing.
02
Learn to read binwalk output properly, including how to carve a specific offset rather than extracting everything.
03
Get comfortable with zsteg bit-plane syntax — knowing what -b 2,8,lsb,xy selects is worth several solves on its own.
04
Keep Audacity installed and know how to switch to spectrogram view. Audio challenges are fast once you can see them.
05
Always run a hex dump on anything that feels wrong. xxd | head catches more than you would expect.
Tools the organisers name for Steganography
binwalkzstegstegsolvesteghideexiftoolAudacity (spectrogram)CyberChefPillow (Python)

03 OSINT Priority 1 open domain

01
Memorise the useful Google operators: site:, filetype:, inurl:, intitle:, quotes for exact phrases, and - to exclude.
02
Learn to read ExifTool output properly — GPS coordinates, timestamps and serial numbers solve more OSINT challenges than any other single tool.
03
Practise geolocation on a blank map. Being able to say "this is eastern UP in October, not the coast" is a real, trainable skill.
04
Get comfortable with the Wayback Machine, including its CDX API for enumerating every snapshot of a URL.
05
Verify before you conclude. Most wrong OSINT answers come from an assumption that was never checked.
Tools the organisers name for OSINT
ExifToolGoogle advanced search operatorsWayback MachineSherlock / MaigretWHOISShodan / CensysReverse image searchSpiderFoot

04 Web Exploitation Priority 2 open domain

01
Work through PortSwigger Web Security Academy end to end — it is free, structured, and maps almost one-to-one onto what the category tests.
02
Set up a local lab with intentionally broken apps: DVWA, Juice Shop and WebGoat. Break them by hand before you try to break a timed challenge.
03
Learn to read application source. Most web challenges ship a snippet, a config or a comment; the vulnerability is nearly always visible once you know where to look.
04
Get fast at reading Burp output — repeater, intruder and the request/response diff are where the actual work happens.
05
Memorise the handful of payloads that matter: a boolean SQLi test, a basic reflected-XSS tag, an SSRF probe, and a JWT alg: none variant.
Tools the organisers name for Web Exploitation
Burp Suite CommunitysqlmapcurlffufwfuzzBrowser DevToolsPython requestsHashcat / John

05 Cryptography Priority 2 open domain

01
Actually implement AES, RSA and a Vigenère cipher from scratch in Python. Writing them is what makes recognising their misuse automatic.
02
Learn to factor small integers quickly and to read n, e, c triples without hesitation — you will be doing it under a clock.
03
Understand padding: PKCS#7, OAEP and ECB-vs-CBC. Most symmetric challenge solves are a padding or mode mistake in disguise.
04
Practise reading sympy output and using discrete_log when a challenge hands you a small group.
05
Keep a scratch file of the ten solves you have done before. Crypto is the one category where muscle memory pays off most.
Tools the organisers name for Cryptography
Python + pycryptodomeSymPySageMathhashcat / John the RipperGnuPGCyberChefRsaCtfToolz3 solver

06 AI / LLM Security Priority 2 open domain

01
Read the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications end to end. It is short, current, and maps almost directly onto these challenges.
02
Follow the published prompt-injection research from Simon Willison and the OWASP GenAI project — this is a category where the reading list is the preparation.
03
Build a local model endpoint you can query in a loop, so you can iterate on a payload in seconds instead of through a browser.
04
Practise multi-turn escalation. Most single-shot injection fails, and most multi-turn escalation succeeds.
05
Understand tokenisation well enough to explain why "spell it backwards" and encoding tricks work — that understanding generalises to every bypass.
Tools the organisers name for AI / LLM Security
curl / httpieBurp SuitePython + openai-compatible clientsGradio / Streamlit (for local models)PromptfooNuclei templatesCustom tokeniser scriptsAnythingLLM / LangChain test rigs

07 Cloud Security Priority 3 open domain

01
Get a free-tier account on one major cloud and build something small. Reading a real IAM policy only makes sense once you have written one.
02
Study the four most common real-world cloud compromises: exposed credentials, permissive storage, SSRF to metadata, and over-privileged CI/CD.
03
Learn the AWS shared-responsibility boundary properly — it explains most of what these challenges are testing.
04
Practise secret scanning with gitleaks or trufflehog against public repositories to see what leaks look like in the wild.
05
Read a Dockerfile and a Kubernetes manifest with a security eye. Insecure defaults are everywhere and worth recognising instantly.
Tools the organisers name for Cloud Security
AWS CLIAzure CLItrufflehog / gitleaksScoutSuite / cloudmapperkube-benchTerraformffuf / nucleiCyberChef

08 Digital Forensics Priority 3 open domain

01
Build a Volidity 3 workflow end to end on a practice image: plugins list, process listing, network scan, file dump. Speed beats novelty in this category.
02
Learn to read a hex dump by hand for the first few bytes. File signatures are the fastest way to identify a carved artefact.
03
Practise timeline questions specifically — most challenges ultimately ask "when" or "in what order".
04
Get comfortable with tshark field filters so you can isolate a conversation instead of scrolling through thousands of packets.
05
Do at least one full forensic writeup end to end. It forces you to record what you examined, which is exactly the discipline the category rewards.
Tools the organisers name for Digital Forensics
Autopsy / The Sleuth KitVolatility 3Wireshark & tsharkbinwalkforemostExifToolFTK Imagerstrings / xxd

09 Reverse Engineering Priority 4 open domain

01
Complete a Ghidra course — the "Intro to Reverse Engineering" free course from the training.github.com Ghidra track is the right starting point.
02
Learn enough x86-64 to read a decompiled function without flinching: calling convention, stack frame, and what rbp-relative reads mean.
03
Always run the binary first. Even when it does nothing useful, strings, its dynamic dependencies and its runtime behaviour tell you what to decompile.
04
Practise on crackmes.one from easy to medium. There is no substitute for the first twenty binaries.
05
Learn the handful of Ghidra shortcuts that matter — rename, retype, force-integer — because manual naming is what makes a function readable.
Tools the organisers name for Reverse Engineering
GhidraIDA Freeradare2 / rizinGDB & pwndbgstrace / ltracex64dbg (Windows)FridaPython + capstone / pyelftools

10 Pwn Priority 4 open domain

01
Complete the classic pwn.college or picoCTF reverse/exploit track. Both are free and structured.
02
Learn pwntools properly rather than scripting by hand — remote, recvuntil and the ROP builder save hours per challenge.
03
Run checksec on every binary before you analyse it. Knowing which mitigations are enabled decides your whole approach.
04
Write the full ret2libc chain at least five times by hand. Once you can do it without documentation, everything above it becomes approachable.
05
Set up Docker so you can pull the challenge binary locally and debug against your own instance instead of the shared server.
Tools the organisers name for Pwn
pwndbg (GDB)pwntoolschecksecROPgadget / ropperGhidraone_gadgetstrace / ltraceDocker (for local instances)

What the five steps have in common

01Recognition first
Almost every step 01 is about learning to see the flaw — implement the cipher, memorise the operator, run the escalation ladder. Tooling comes later.
02Speed under a clock
Step 02 is consistently about doing the recognition fast: factor small integers quickly, read n, e, c without hesitation.
03The specific gotcha
Step 03 names the mistake the category is built on — padding, misconfigured IAM, an exposed metadata endpoint.
04Deliberate practice
Step 04 points at a free structured resource — PortSwigger Academy, CryptoHack, pwn.college, a Ghidra course.
05Muscle memory
Step 05 is nearly always “keep a scratch file” or “build a workflow”. On the 17th, recall will fail — retrieval will not.
◆Not required to enter
The organisers state plainly on every page: none of this is required to enter. It is simply the shortest path to scoring.

Deliberately excluded

These come up in CTF culture and are a poor use of three days. Each is excluded on purpose.
Do not spend time onDomainWhy it is a trap
Heap exploitation (ptmalloc)PwnRequires weeks of allocator internals. Not reachable in three days, and the organisers' own guidance says basic only.
Full ROP chain constructionPwnDepends on stack overflow plus gadget hunting plus mitigation bypass. Each layer is a session of its own.
Custom algorithm reimplementationReverse EngineeringHigh effort, and usually gated behind obfuscation you must defeat first.
Windows registry deep-diveForensicsLower frequency on student boards than disk, memory and network artifacts.
Kernel exploitationPwnNot in scope for a Jeopardy student competition.
Advanced cryptanalysis (differential, lattice)CryptographyThe board's crypto points are parameter bugs — small e, factorable n, padding. Not mathematics.
Active directory attacksCloudDifferent discipline entirely; not one of the ten published categories.
Length-extension chainingCryptographyWorth one session at most. Do not build a day around it.

Every practice item on this page, in one place. 57 full walkthroughs from the two PDFs — complete with the exact steps, what you should see, and why it matters — plus 123 curated drills. All 180 items are tagged by domain and mapped to the official Ghost Protocol sub-type they train. Nothing here is off-syllabus.
